c.tagline: Brazil's northeastern capital of bridges, beaches, frevo and colonial Olinda.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered; airport 'Special Taxis' (Táxi Especial) charge a set fare by zone, and ride-hailing apps are usually cheaper than street taxis.

emergency.note: 193 reaches the fire brigade; 190 is the military police. Dialing 192 summons SAMU ambulances.

avoid.reason: Elevated street crime; caution in Boa Viagem after dark and central/port areas

hood_desc: Recife's upscale beachfront district: a long crescent of sand backed by a busy boardwalk, high-rise hotels and the Shopping Recife mall. It is the safest and most convenient base for most visitors, with the airport and metro close by. (Swim with care — reef-edge waters here carry a shark-attack risk, so heed the flagged signs.)

The historic island quarter (Bairro do Recife) where the city was born, with cobbled streets, colourful colonial facades, the Marco Zero square, Paço do Frevo and Cais do Sertão museums, and a lively bar-and-restaurant nightlife scene after dark.

The old commercial heart of downtown alongside São José and Boa Vista, packed with baroque churches, the Santa Isabel Theatre, Praça da República and street markets — a gritty, authentic slice of everyday Recife best explored by day.
A calm, leafy upper-middle-class residential neighbourhood that is safe and central, dotted with good bars, bakeries and restaurants and within easy reach of downtown, Boa Viagem and Olinda.

The UNESCO-listed colonial hill town just north of Recife, famous for its pastel casario, baroque churches, artists' studios, sweeping viewpoints and one of Brazil's most authentic frevo-and-maracatu street carnivals.

transit.hours: The Metrô runs roughly 5am to 11pm daily; there is no all-night rail service, so late-night travellers rely on buses or ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: Recife's rail backbone is the CBTU-run Metrô (MetroRec) — two electrified lines plus a diesel VLT branch — feeding a large municipal and metropolitan bus network (Grande Recife Consórcio de Transporte); ferries and catamarans also cross the rivers in the old center.
transit.pay: Buy and top up a rechargeable VEM card (Vale Eletrônico Metropolitano) for buses and the Metrô, or pay cash to bus drivers; a single Metrô ride costs about R$4.25 (~$0.85).

ferry: River catamarans and Cais do Sertão crossings in the old center

transit.m: Metrô (Linha Sul) from Aeroporto station to the center (~35 min)
Special Taxi (set fare) or ride-hail to Boa Viagem / center (20-35 min)

tip.r: 10% service is usually already added to restaurant bills; extra tipping is optional.

food.name: Carne de sol
food.desc: Sun-cured beef from the sertao, grilled and served with macaxeira (cassava), butter cheese and pirao. The benchmark plate of Pernambuco cooking.

places.name: Parraxaxa
places.note: Sertao-themed regional buffet locals send visitors to for carne de sol and cassava sides.

places.name: Seu Luna
places.note: Long-running northeastern kitchen famed for slow-cooked regional meats and mao de vaca.

places.name: Restaurante Leite
places.note: Recife's grand old dining room, open since 1882, for a formal take on regional classics.

food.name: Tapioca
food.desc: Cassava-starch crepe cooked on a griddle and folded over queijo coalho, carne de sol or coconut and condensed milk. Breakfast and late-night staple.

places.name: Tapioqueiras do Alto da Se
places.note: Row of veteran tapioca stalls with hilltop views over Recife; the classic pilgrimage.

places.name: Mercado da Boa Vista
places.note: Working market with stalls griddling tapiocas and cuscuz for market-goers all morning.

places.name: Parraxaxa
places.note: Live tapioca station at the regional breakfast buffet, good if you want many fillings.

food.name: Caldinho de feijao
food.desc: Silky blended black-bean broth served scalding in a small glass, dusted with parsley and often spiked with cachaca. The standard bar snack of Recife.

places.name: Bar Central
places.note: Beloved old-school boteco where petiscos and caldinhos come with cold draught beer.

places.name: Barracas da Praia de Boa Viagem
places.note: Beach kiosks along Avenida Boa Viagem serve caldinho by the glass all afternoon.

places.name: Seu Boteco
places.note: Popular neighbourhood bar with a broad petisco list including bean and shrimp caldinhos.

food.name: Agulha frita
food.desc: Slim needlefish fried whole until crisp and eaten with lime and a cold beer. Sold from beach barracas and market fry stalls up and down the coast.

places.name: Mercado de Sao Jose
places.note: Brazil's oldest iron-framed market (1875); fish stalls and fry counters under one roof.

places.name: Barracas da Praia de Boa Viagem
places.note: Fried fish served straight to the sand, the way locals eat it on weekends.

places.name: Mercado do Pina
places.note: Neighbourhood fish market with simple bars frying the morning's catch to order.

food.name: Bolo de rolo
food.desc: Pernambuco's protected cake: paper-thin sponge layers rolled around guava paste, sliced into fine spirals. Bought by the log to take home.

places.name: Casa dos Frios
places.note: Long-standing deli and bakery locals rely on for bolo de rolo and regional sweets.

places.name: Mercado de Sao Jose
places.note: Sweet stalls sell boxed bolo de rolo alongside cocada and doce de leite.

places.name: Mercado de Casa Amarela
places.note: Big residential market where bakers sell homemade bolo de rolo by weight.

food.name: Cartola
food.desc: Fried ripe banana layered with melted queijo de manteiga and showered in cinnamon sugar. Pernambuco's simplest and best-loved dessert.

places.name: Parraxaxa
places.note: Regional dessert table always includes cartola made to order.

places.name: Seu Luna
places.note: Traditional northeastern menu that finishes with cartola and bolo de rolo.

places.name: Restaurante Leite
places.note: Historic house version of the dish, served with the city's oldest dining-room ceremony.

food.name: Caipirinha de cachaca pernambucana
food.desc: Lime, sugar and local cane spirit such as Pitu, distilled just outside Recife. Ask for versions made with caja, umbu or passionfruit instead of lime.

places.name: Bar Central
places.note: Cachaca-forward boteco with a deep list of Pernambuco distillates.

places.name: Mercado de Sao Jose
places.note: Cachaca stalls pour tastings of artisanal Pernambuco brands by the shot.

places.name: Seu Boteco
places.note: Reliable bar for fruit caipirinhas with beach-side petiscos after dark.

food.name: Agua de coco and caldo de cana
food.desc: Chilled green coconut water drunk straight from the shell, or freshly pressed sugarcane juice with lime. The everyday non-alcoholic pair in Recife.

places.name: Barracas da Praia de Boa Viagem
places.note: Vendors machete open coconuts along the whole beach promenade.

places.name: Mercado da Boa Vista
places.note: Cane presses at the market entrance turn out caldo de cana all day.

places.name: Parque Dona Lindu kiosks
places.note: Seafront park kiosks pouring coconut water beside the Niemeyer towers.

landmarks: Marco Zero (Praça do Marco Zero)
The symbolic 'zero point' plaza in Recife Antigo, with its striking spiral pavement design, marks the historic birthplace of the city.
Rua do Bom Jesus (Recife Antigo)
A postcard row of vividly painted colonial buildings in the historic old town, home to the first synagogue in the Americas.
Instituto Ricardo Brennand
A fairytale-like medieval-style castle and museum housing one of the world's finest collections of arms, armor, and Dutch colonial-era art.
Casa da Cultura de Pernambuco
A former 19th-century prison ingeniously repurposed into a vibrant crafts market, its cell-block architecture is uniquely photogenic.
Basílica e Convento do Carmo
An ornate Baroque church and convent complex whose gilded interior and grand facade reflect Recife's rich religious heritage.
Torre Malakoff
A distinctive octagonal 19th-century observation tower on the waterfront, once used for astronomical and meteorological observation.
Boa Viagem Beach
Recife's iconic urban beach, framed by a long curve of high-rise towers and coconut palms, is the city's most famous stretch of coastline.
Paço do Frevo
A museum dedicated to frevo, Recife's UNESCO-recognized musical and dance tradition, set in a beautifully restored historic building.
Capela Dourada (Golden Chapel)
A dazzling 17th-century chapel entirely covered in gold-leafed woodcarving, considered one of Brazil's finest Baroque interiors.
Sinagoga Kahal Zur Israel
The first synagogue built in the Americas, this 17th-century Dutch-Jewish landmark is a unique piece of New World religious history.

train.note: No intercity passenger trains. Recife has the Metrô do Recife, a suburban rail network run by CBTU that reaches Jaboatão and Cabo, but it is urban transit rather than long-distance travel. Everything beyond the metropolitan area goes by coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. The TIP (Terminal Integrado de Passageiros) is well outside the centre but connected by metro. Progresso, Real Alagoas and Itapemirim-successor operators run to Maceió (about 4 hours), João Pessoa (2), Natal (4) and Salvador (12); book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/).

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Recife. The port handles cargo and cruise calls, and catamarans across the Capibaribe and out to the reefs are sightseeing trips. Boats to the island of Fernando de Noronha do not exist as a passenger service - the island is reached by air.

half.name: Porto de Galinhas
half.blurb: A beach town about an hour and a half south has calm reef-protected pools and natural tide pools reachable by jangada boat.

half.name: Itamaracá Island
half.blurb: An island about an hour north connects by bridge and holds the ruins of Fort Orange and a manatee conservation center.

half.name: Igarassu
half.blurb: A colonial town about 40 minutes north preserves Brazil's oldest church, built by Franciscan friars in the mid-16th century.

full.name: Caruaru
full.blurb: An inland market city about two hours away is known for its forró music, leather crafts, and clay figurine artisans.
